title: Key exchange: Diffie-Hellman and forward secrecy

videos.script: Lesson 3 got a key to the other side by encrypting it with the other side's public key. There is a better way, and every modern protocol uses it. {{title}} Two parties each pick a secret number. Each sends something computed from it, in the open. Each then combines what it received with its own secret. They end up with the same value, and nobody listening can compute it. {{exchange}} That is Diffie-Hellman, from 1976, and today it runs on the curve X25519. {{x25519}} Its best property shows up a year later. If a server's long-term key leaks, recorded traffic protected by that key can be read. Traffic protected by a fresh exchange cannot, because the exchange keys are already gone. {{fs}} But an exchange alone does not say who is on the other end. {{mitm}} And a large quantum computer would break it, which is why new algorithms are already being deployed beside it. {{pq}}
